case.label: C
case.text: C needs no application code change at all and no redeployment, which a reader could match to 'without a new deployment'. It fails on overhead: someone must schedule and maintain the script, restart the application, and instances that Auto Scaling launches later still get the old file. B is a one-time small code change, which the stem explicitly accepts, and rotation then needs no further work. A goes stale after the first rotation on long-lived instances, and D fails because Parameter Store has no built-in rotation.

case.label: A
case.text: A works in the standard tier and avoids the advanced-tier charge and the one-way tier change, so a cost-minded reader could prefer it. But the stem asks for LEAST operational overhead, and a custom Lambda function plus SNS is code to maintain. Parameter policies such as NoChangeNotification require the advanced tier, so B is not possible, and D's Expiration policy (also advanced-only) measures time to a fixed date, not time since the last update.

case.label: D
case.text: D keeps the same CA and also works, because an ALB listener can use a certificate from the IAM certificate store. It adds overhead (a second certificate store and a listener change) and gives up ACM expiry monitoring, so B, which reimports to the same ARN and keeps the existing listener association, is lower overhead. ACM does not renew imported certificates (C), and the validation method of an imported certificate cannot be changed (A).

case.label: D
case.text: D, together with C, also gives the function access, and a candidate who reads only 'which steps work' could pick it. The stem says MOST securely, and D grants every principal in account B instead of the one role, so A is the least-privilege choice. B is impossible because the key policy of an AWS managed key cannot be edited, and E is wrong because a secret's resource-based policy cannot grant kms:Decrypt on the key.

case.label: A
case.text: A describes a real feature (exportable public ACM certificates), so it is technically possible and does renew in ACM. It still needs a script on every instance after each renewal and on every new instance from scale-out, so its overhead is much higher than D, where the load balancer terminates TLS and ACM renews in place. Wording cue: D is the only option that names DNS validation, which the Route 53 and auto-renew lines of the stem point at.

case.label: A
case.text: A NAT gateway also fixes the failure, and the rotation code would need no change. But the traffic then leaves through the internet path, and the stem states a preference for private connectivity and asks for MOST securely, so the interface endpoint wins. B fails because gateway endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. A small unstated detail in D: the endpoint needs private DNS enabled (the default) so the SDK's normal Secrets Manager hostname resolves to it.

case.label: B
case.text: B looks like a fast workaround, but while the old secret is scheduled for deletion its name stays reserved, and a new secret gets a new ARN with a new random suffix, so the IAM policies that name the old ARN would no longer match. Restoring inside the default recovery window keeps the same ARN and value, so A is faster and complete. C fails because a secret scheduled for deletion cannot be read.

case.label: D
case.text: D also gives us-west-2 a local copy without depending on us-east-1 at read time, and a reader might like that it keeps two independent secrets. It is custom code with a timing gap after each rotation, so C (native replication, with rotation on the primary updating the replica) has less overhead. Note: the standby can read the replica without promoting it; promotion in C is needed only to write or rotate in us-west-2 after a failover, so the extra step does not make C wrong.

case.label: D
case.text: D is the cheapest storage option and a candidate could read 'change the parameter value when required' as meeting the 30-day policy by hand. The stem says the password must be rotated automatically, and Parameter Store has no built-in rotation, so D and A fail that requirement (NoChangeNotification only notifies). Between the Secrets Manager options, C avoids the monthly charge of a customer managed KMS key, so C is more cost-effective than B.

case.label: B
case.text: B also places a valid certificate in US East (N. Virginia), which is the Region CloudFront requires, so it works. It adds a purchase, a manual import and manual renewal, so A is lower overhead. C fails because an ACM certificate cannot be copied to another Region, and D fails because CloudFront cannot use a certificate from eu-west-1. Out of scope for every option: CloudFront-to-ALB HTTPS also needs the origin certificate to match the origin domain or forwarded Host header, but no option changes that.

case.label: D
case.text: Email validation does validate the domain, and a reader could think renewal is automatic once the first email is approved. ACM managed renewal of an email-validated certificate still sends an email that a person must approve, which breaks 'no action from a person at renewal time'. DNS validation with the CNAME kept in the Route 53 hosted zone renews with no action. B gives up managed renewal entirely, and A describes a validation flow that the load balancer does not provide.

case.label: B
case.text: B keeps the shared CA and ends with the certificate on the HTTPS listener, so it encrypts in transit. A certificate imported into ACM is not renewed by ACM, so someone must reissue and reimport it before expiry, which is more overhead than A, where ACM requests and renews the private certificate from the shared CA. C adds a CA and breaks the isolation design, and D moves TLS work to every target.

case.label: C
case.text: C adds encryption and a review reminder, which a security-minded reader might prefer for any configuration value. The value is a non-secret endpoint URL that changes by hand, so encryption and rotation are not required, and the advanced tier and Secrets Manager (A, D) all add cost. A standard String parameter has no storage charge, so B is the most cost-effective option.
